subproblem.title: The open unit cube in Euclid k has Lebesgue measure 1
subproblem.statement: For every k ∈ ℕ, the open unit cube Q₁ := {y ∈ Euclid k : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i ∈ Fin k} in Euclid k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) has Lebesgue measure volume(Q₁) = 1 (as an element of [0, ∞]).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ k : ℕ, volume {y : Euclid k | ∀ i, 0 < y i ∧ y i < 1} = 1
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: the notation paragraph of the parent proof ('Under the measure-preserving linear isometry Euclid n ≃ (Fin n → ℝ) ... Q_δ corresponds to the box ∏_i (δ, 1 − δ), so ... vol(Q₁) = 1'). Here it is specialized to δ = 0 and stated for every dimension k.

Let k ∈ ℕ and Q₁ := {y ∈ Euclid k : 0 < y_i < 1 for all i ∈ Fin k}. Here y_i = y i is the i-th coordinate, i.e. the i-th component of WithLp.ofLp y ∈ (Fin k → ℝ).

1. Let B := ∏_{i ∈ Fin k} (0, 1) = Set.univ.pi (fun _ => Set.Ioo 0 1) ⊆ (Fin k → ℝ). B is measurable because it is a finite product of open intervals (MeasurableSet.univ_pi, measurableSet_Ioo). In particular it is null-measurable.
2. The coordinate map ofLp : Euclid k → (Fin k → ℝ) is measure preserving, from the volume (Lebesgue measure) of Euclid k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) to the product Lebesgue measure on Fin k → ℝ (Mathlib PiLp.volume_preserving_ofLp (Fin k); equivalently EuclideanSpace.volume_preserving_symm_measurableEquiv_toLp).
3. Q₁ = ofLp⁻¹(B). For y ∈ Euclid k: y ∈ Q₁ ⟺ ∀ i, 0 < (ofLp y) i ∧ (ofLp y) i < 1 ⟺ ∀ i, (ofLp y) i ∈ Ioo 0 1 ⟺ ofLp y ∈ B (Set.mem_pi; in Lean, ext y; simp [Set.mem_pi]).
4. Applying step 2 to the null-measurable set B (MeasurePreserving.measure_preimage) gives volume(Q₁) = volume(ofLp⁻¹(B)) = volume(B).
5. By the product formula for open boxes (Real.volume_pi_Ioo), volume(B) = ∏_{i ∈ Fin k} ENNReal.ofReal(1 − 0) = ∏_{i ∈ Fin k} 1 = 1. When k = 0 this is the empty product, which is also 1.
6. By steps 4 and 5, volume(Q₁) = 1. ∎
proof_key_steps: Q₁ is the preimage of the box B = ∏_i (0,1) under the coordinate map ofLp : Euclid k → (Fin k → ℝ).
ofLp is measure preserving (PiLp.volume_preserving_ofLp), so vol(Q₁) = vol(B) because B is measurable.
vol(B) = ∏_i ofReal(1 − 0) = 1 by Real.volume_pi_Ioo (the empty product when k = 0).

audit.reason: The prose and exact Lean proposition agree for every natural dimension. The measurable product box is precisely the coordinate-map preimage defining the cube. Volume preservation and the open-box product formula prove the conclusion, including the empty product when k = 0. This independently supplies the parent's probability normalization.

subproblem.title: An integer-valued a.e.-measurable function on a probability space has an integer median
subproblem.statement: Let X be a measurable space and μ a probability measure on X. Let u : X → ℝ be μ-a.e.-measurable with u(x) ∈ ℤ for every x ∈ X. Then there is β ∈ ℤ with μ{x : β ≤ u(x)} ≥ 1/2 and μ{x : u(x) ≤ β} ≥ 1/2, where μ(A) denotes the real number μ.real A = (μ A).toReal.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [MeasurableSpace X] (μ : Measure X) (u : X → ℝ), IsProbabilityMeasure μ → AEMeasurable u μ → (∀ x, ∃ z : ℤ, u x = z) → ∃ β : ℤ, 1 / 2 ≤ μ.real {x | (β : ℝ) ≤ u x} ∧ 1 / 2 ≤ μ.real {x | u x ≤ (β : ℝ)}
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 0–2 of the parent proof, i.e. the integer median choice (31) in Simon's proof of Ch. 6, 5.1 (book/chapter-06.txt lines 1879–1883: take β with min{Lⁿ{F ≥ β}, Lⁿ{F ≤ β}} ≥ 1/2, and β ∈ ℤ when F is integer-valued). The parent's step 0 explicitly allows working with the μ-null-measurable sets {u ≤ t}; we do so instead of passing to a Borel representative.

Notation. For A ⊆ X write μ(A) for the real number μ.real A = (μ A).toReal ∈ [0, 1]. For t ∈ ℝ put F(t) := μ{x : u(x) ≤ t}.

1. Null-measurability and complements. u is μ-a.e.-measurable and (−∞, t] is a Borel set, so each {u ≤ t} = u⁻¹((−∞, t]) is μ-null-measurable (AEMeasurable.nullMeasurableSet_preimage with measurableSet_Iic). Since μ is a probability measure, μ(Aᶜ) = 1 − μ(A) for every μ-null-measurable A (probReal_compl_eq_one_sub₀).
2. Monotonicity. μ is finite, so A ⊆ B implies μ(A) ≤ μ(B) (measureReal_mono). If s ≤ t then {u ≤ s} ⊆ {u ≤ t}, so F is nondecreasing.
3. Upper tail: S is nonempty. For n ∈ ℕ let A_n := {u ≤ n}.
   - The sequence (A_n) is increasing, and ⋃_n A_n = X because every real number u(x) is at most some natural number (exists_nat_ge).
   - Continuity of measure from below holds for any increasing sequence of sets (tendsto_measure_iUnion_atTop). So μ A_n → μ X = 1 in [0, ∞].
   - Since toReal is continuous at the finite value 1 (ENNReal.tendsto_toReal), F(n) = μ(A_n) → 1 in ℝ.
   - As 1/2 < 1, there is n₁ ∈ ℕ with F(n₁) > 1/2, so in particular F(n₁) ≥ 1/2.
   Hence S := {z ∈ ℤ : F(z) ≥ 1/2} contains the integer n₁ and is nonempty.
4. Lower tail. For n ∈ ℕ let B_n := {u ≤ −n}.
   - The sequence (B_n) is decreasing. Each B_n is μ-null-measurable (step 1) and has finite measure.
   - ⋂_n B_n = ∅: for each x there is n ∈ ℕ with n > −u(x) (exists_nat_gt), i.e. u(x) > −n, so x ∉ B_n.
   - By continuity of measure from above (tendsto_measure_iInter_atTop), μ B_n → μ ∅ = 0. Hence F(−n) = μ(B_n) → 0 in ℝ (ENNReal.tendsto_toReal).
   - As 0 < 1/2, there is n₀ ∈ ℕ with F(−n₀) < 1/2.
5. S is bounded below by −n₀. Let z ∈ S and suppose z < −n₀. Then z ≤ −n₀, also as real numbers, so step 2 gives F(z) ≤ F(−n₀) < 1/2. This contradicts F(z) ≥ 1/2. Hence −n₀ ≤ z for every z ∈ S.
6. Choice of β. By steps 3 and 5, S is a nonempty set of integers that is bounded below, so it has a least element β (Int.exists_least_of_bdd). Since β ∈ S, μ{u ≤ β} = F(β) ≥ 1/2. This is the second claim.
7. β − 1 ∉ S, because otherwise minimality of β would give β ≤ β − 1. Hence F(β − 1) = μ{u ≤ β − 1} < 1/2.
8. Integer values. Let x ∈ X and choose z ∈ ℤ with u(x) = z. For integers, β ≤ z ⟺ β − 1 < z ⟺ ¬(z ≤ β − 1). Casting to ℝ (Int.cast_le, Int.cast_lt) gives β ≤ u(x) ⟺ ¬(u(x) ≤ β − 1). Hence {x : β ≤ u(x)} = {x : u(x) ≤ β − 1}ᶜ.
9. By steps 8, 1 and 7, μ{β ≤ u} = 1 − μ{u ≤ β − 1} = 1 − F(β − 1) > 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. In particular μ{β ≤ u} ≥ 1/2. This is the first claim.
By steps 6 and 9, β ∈ ℤ has both required properties. ∎
proof_key_steps: Each {u ≤ t} is μ-null-measurable, so μ(Aᶜ) = 1 − μ(A) for these sets; F(t) = μ{u ≤ t} is nondecreasing.
Continuity from below on {u ≤ n} gives F(n₁) > 1/2, so S = {z ∈ ℤ : F(z) ≥ 1/2} is nonempty.
Continuity from above on the null-measurable decreasing sets {u ≤ −n} gives F(−n₀) < 1/2, so S is bounded below by −n₀.
β := min S (Int.exists_least_of_bdd) satisfies μ{u ≤ β} ≥ 1/2 and μ{u ≤ β − 1} < 1/2.
Integer values give {β ≤ u} = {u ≤ β − 1}ᶜ, so μ{β ≤ u} = 1 − F(β − 1) > 1/2.

audit.reason: The type includes every stated hypothesis and both real-valued median inequalities. A.e. measurability supplies null-measurable level sets; probability supplies finiteness and complement identities. The two tail limits establish a nonempty, bounded-below integer threshold set. Its least element and integer-valuedness give the required complementary half-mass bound. Every step is justified without assuming integrability or invoking the parent.

subproblem.title: A median is at most twice the mean absolute value
subproblem.statement: Let X be a measurable space, μ a probability measure on X, u : X → ℝ μ-integrable, and β ∈ ℝ with μ{x : β ≤ u(x)} ≥ 1/2 and μ{x : u(x) ≤ β} ≥ 1/2, where μ(A) := μ.real A. Then |β| ≤ 2 ∫_X |u| dμ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [MeasurableSpace X] (μ : Measure X) (u : X → ℝ) (β : ℝ), IsProbabilityMeasure μ → Integrable u μ → 1 / 2 ≤ μ.real {x | β ≤ u x} → 1 / 2 ≤ μ.real {x | u x ≤ β} → |β| ≤ 2 * ∫ x, |u x| ∂μ
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof, i.e. the bound (35) |β_F| ≤ 2∫_F |F| dLⁿ in Simon's proof of Ch. 6, 5.1 (book/chapter-06.txt lines 1906–1908). Simon deduces it from the median choice (31). The parent's case β = 0 is absorbed into case (a) below.

Notation. μ(A) := μ.real A for A ⊆ X.

1. Markov's inequality. |u| is nonnegative and μ-integrable (Integrable.abs). With ε := |β| ≥ 0, we have ε·μ{x : ε ≤ |u(x)|} ≤ ∫|u| dμ (mul_meas_ge_le_integral_of_nonneg). Mathematically:
   - ε·1_{ε ≤ |u|} ≤ |u| pointwise because ε ≥ 0;
   - the set {ε ≤ |u|} is μ-null-measurable because u is a.e.-measurable;
   - integrating the pointwise bound gives the inequality.
2. Claim: μ{x : |β| ≤ |u(x)|} ≥ 1/2. Since μ is finite, μ is monotone under inclusion (measureReal_mono).
   (a) If β ≥ 0: for every x with β ≤ u(x), |β| = β ≤ u(x) ≤ |u(x)|. Hence {β ≤ u} ⊆ {|β| ≤ |u|}, and μ{|β| ≤ |u|} ≥ μ{β ≤ u} ≥ 1/2 by hypothesis.
   (b) If β < 0: for every x with u(x) ≤ β, |β| = −β ≤ −u(x) ≤ |u(x)|. Hence {u ≤ β} ⊆ {|β| ≤ |u|}, and μ{|β| ≤ |u|} ≥ μ{u ≤ β} ≥ 1/2 by hypothesis.
3. By steps 1 and 2 and |β| ≥ 0, |β|·(1/2) ≤ |β|·μ{|β| ≤ |u|} ≤ ∫|u| dμ. Multiplying by 2 gives |β| ≤ 2∫|u| dμ. ∎
proof_key_steps: Markov's inequality for |u| at level |β|: |β|·μ{|β| ≤ |u|} ≤ ∫|u| dμ.
If β ≥ 0 then {β ≤ u} ⊆ {|β| ≤ |u|}; if β < 0 then {u ≤ β} ⊆ {|β| ≤ |u|}. Either way μ{|β| ≤ |u|} ≥ 1/2.

audit.reason: The prose and Lean type agree. Markov's inequality applies to the integrable nonnegative function |u| at level |β|. The sign cases correctly place a median half-mass set inside {|β| ≤ |u|}; finite-measure monotonicity then gives |β|/2 ≤ ∫|u|. The proof includes β = 0 and requires neither another child nor the parent theorem.

subproblem.title: A median minimizes the mean absolute deviation
subproblem.statement: Let X be a measurable space, μ a probability measure on X, u : X → ℝ μ-integrable, and β ∈ ℝ a median of u: μ{x : β ≤ u(x)} ≥ 1/2 and μ{x : u(x) ≤ β} ≥ 1/2, where μ(A) := μ.real A. Then ∫_X |u − β| dμ ≤ ∫_X |u − c| dμ for every c ∈ ℝ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [MeasurableSpace X] (μ : Measure X) (u : X → ℝ) (β : ℝ), IsProbabilityMeasure μ → Integrable u μ → 1 / 2 ≤ μ.real {x | β ≤ u x} → 1 / 2 ≤ μ.real {x | u x ≤ β} → ∀ c : ℝ, ∫ x, |u x - β| ∂μ ≤ ∫ x, |u x - c| ∂μ
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 3 of the parent proof, the minimality of the median β. This minimizing property is what replaces the median hypothesis of Simon Ch. 2, 2.7. It is the classical fact that a median minimizes c ↦ E|u − c|; the pointwise comparison argument of the parent is used.

Notation. μ(A) := μ.real A for A ⊆ X; 1_s denotes the indicator of s (value 1 on s, 0 off s). Fix c ∈ ℝ.

1. Integrability. For every a ∈ ℝ, x ↦ |u(x) − a| is μ-integrable. Indeed u is integrable, the constant a is integrable because μ is finite (integrable_const), and differences and absolute values of integrable functions are integrable (Integrable.sub, Integrable.abs).
2. Null-measurability. u is integrable, hence μ-a.e.-measurable (Integrable.aemeasurable). So the sets {u ≤ β} = u⁻¹((−∞, β]) and {β ≤ u} = u⁻¹([β, ∞)) are μ-null-measurable (AEMeasurable.nullMeasurableSet_preimage with measurableSet_Iic, measurableSet_Ici).
3. Indicator integrals. Let s be μ-null-measurable.
   - 1_s is integrable: apply IntegrableOn.integrable_indicator₀ to the constant 1, which is integrable on the finite measure μ.
   - ∫ 1_s dμ = ∫_s 1 dμ = μ(s) (integral_indicator₀, setIntegral_const).
   - ∫ 1 dμ = μ(X) = 1 (integral_const, probReal_univ).
4. Key lemma. Let s be μ-null-measurable with μ(s) ≥ 1/2, let d ≥ 0, and assume the pointwise bound d·(2·1_s(x) − 1) ≤ |u(x) − c| − |u(x) − β| for all x ∈ X.
   - Both sides are integrable (steps 1 and 3).
   - By monotonicity (integral_mono) and linearity (integral_sub, integral_const_mul) of the integral, together with step 3: d·(2μ(s) − 1) = ∫ d·(2·1_s − 1) dμ ≤ ∫ (|u − c| − |u − β|) dμ = ∫|u − c| dμ − ∫|u − β| dμ.
   - Since d ≥ 0 and 2μ(s) − 1 ≥ 0, the left side is ≥ 0. Hence ∫|u − β| dμ ≤ ∫|u − c| dμ.
5. Case c ≥ β. Apply step 4 with s := {u ≤ β} and d := c − β ≥ 0. Here s is null-measurable by step 2 and μ(s) ≥ 1/2 by hypothesis. Pointwise check:
   (a) If u(x) ≤ β, then u(x) ≤ β ≤ c, so |u(x) − c| = c − u(x) and |u(x) − β| = β − u(x). Hence |u(x) − c| − |u(x) − β| = c − β = d·(2·1 − 1).
   (b) If u(x) > β, then 1_s(x) = 0. By the triangle inequality (abs_sub_le), |u(x) − β| ≤ |u(x) − c| + |c − β| = |u(x) − c| + (c − β). So |u(x) − c| − |u(x) − β| ≥ −(c − β) = d·(2·0 − 1).
6. Case c < β. Apply step 4 with s := {β ≤ u} and d := β − c > 0. Here s is null-measurable by step 2 and μ(s) ≥ 1/2 by hypothesis. Pointwise check:
   (a) If β ≤ u(x), then c < β ≤ u(x), so |u(x) − c| = u(x) − c and |u(x) − β| = u(x) − β. Hence |u(x) − c| − |u(x) − β| = β − c = d·(2·1 − 1).
   (b) If u(x) < β, then 1_s(x) = 0. By the triangle inequality, |u(x) − β| ≤ |u(x) − c| + |c − β| = |u(x) − c| + (β − c). So |u(x) − c| − |u(x) − β| ≥ −(β − c) = d·(2·0 − 1).
7. Steps 5 and 6 cover every c ∈ ℝ, so ∫|u − β| dμ ≤ ∫|u − c| dμ for all c. ∎
proof_key_steps: Every |u − a| is integrable, and so are the indicators of the null-measurable sets {u ≤ β} and {β ≤ u}; ∫1_s dμ = μ(s) and ∫1 dμ = 1.
Key lemma: if d ≥ 0, μ(s) ≥ 1/2 and d(2·1_s − 1) ≤ |u − c| − |u − β| pointwise, then integrating gives ∫|u − c| − ∫|u − β| ≥ d(2μ(s) − 1) ≥ 0.
Case c ≥ β: take s = {u ≤ β}, d = c − β; on s the difference equals c − β, and off s the triangle inequality gives ≥ −(c − β).
Case c < β: take s = {β ≤ u}, d = β − c; on s the difference equals β − c, and off s the triangle inequality gives ≥ −(β − c).

audit.reason: The exact type matches the probability, integrability and two median hypotheses. The proof establishes integrability of deviations and indicators before applying integral monotonicity and linearity. Both cases for c verify the pointwise lower bound and yield minimality. The argument is complete and independent; the cited [Geyer slides, 12–15](https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/f11/5101/slides/s4a.pdf) also document this comparison.
